name: Joe Burrow
blurb1: Burrow attended Athens High School in Athens, Ohio and then started his college career at Ohio State before becoming a graduate transfer to LSU. At Athens High, he was selected as Ohio Mr. Football and passed for 11,400 yards and 157 touchdowns for his career in addition to 2,000 yards rushing with 27 rushing touchdowns. He led his team to seven playoff victories over his three years. Burrow comes from a football family and his father Jimmy and two older brothers Jamie and Dan all played football at Nebraska. His father also coached at Iowa State, Nebraska, North Dakota State and Ohio. Burrow was also a First team All-State point guard in high school and turned down basketball scholarship offers. After earning just a 78.8 PFF passing grade in his first year at LSU after transferring from Ohio State, Burrow recorded the best single-season PFF passing grade (94.1) of any FBS quarterback in the PFF College era (2014-19) this past season. He recorded a 94.9 PFF passing grade from a clean pocket and an 80.5 PFF passing grade under pressure, both of which ranked among the best quarterbacks in the country. He also recorded the highest percentage of on-target passes in PFF’s advanced ball location charting of any quarterback since we started the process in 2016.
blurb2: If you're trying to find negatives for Burrow in his 2019 tape, it's difficult to find any sort of flaw that showed up repeatedly. That comes with the territory of having the best statistical season in college football history. Yes, he made some bad decisions and took some bad sacks at times, but everyone does. Burrow has pinpoint accuracy and maneuvers the pocket as well as any QB prospect I've ever seen. He can make plays inside and outside of structure. He throws with anticipation play after play and will give his guys chances in one-on-one situations. He is the unquestioned top QB in the draft.

name: Anthony Gordon
blurb1: Anthony Gordon was a record-setting quarterback at Terra Nova High School in California, but he still didn’t draw a ton of Division I interest coming out of preps in 2015. He opted for San Francisco’s City College following his senior season at Terra Nova and led the team to a 12-1 record as a freshman. Per Washington State’s official athletic site, Gordon led the CCCAA with 3,864 passing yards and 37 touchdowns that season. Mike Leach and the Cougars took interest in Gordon soon after his epic freshman campaign at City College. Gordon took over the reins to Leach’s air raid system from Gardner Minshew in his sole year as starter, and his box score stats benefited from the scheme, as he completed 91 passes more than any other quarterback and threw for 5,563 yards. His performance on a throw-to-throw basis, though, was above average at best. He did finish with an 81.8 passing grade that tied for 23rd on the year but put the ball in harm’s way far too often as he ranked 60th in turnover-worthy play rate. blurb1: A consensus three-star recruit in 2016, Justin Herbert played basketball, baseball and football at a high level at Oregon’s Sheldon High School. He suffered a season-ending leg injury three games into his junior season at quarterback for the Irish, a break in his femur right above the growth plate that required surgery soon after, per Jerry Ulmer of the Oregonian. He returned to the field and the mound as a senior at Sheldon, accumulating a 1.98 ERA with 39 strikeouts in 42.1 innings pitched while also throwing for over 3,000 yards and 37 touchdowns. Herbert’s decision to commit to Oregon was an easy one. A lifelong fan of the Ducks and season-ticket holder at the time, he chose Oregon over offers from Montana State, Nevada, NAU and Portland State shortly after coach Mark Helfrich offered him a scholarship in October 2015. name: Jalen Hurts
blurb1: Hurts was a four-star prospect coming out of Channelview High School in Channelview, Texas, back in 2016 where his father was his head coach his entire career. While there, he also competed in powerlifting, which is a combo you don't see too often. He ultimately chose Alabama over Texas A&M prior to his senior season. He graduated from Alabama last December with a degree in communications in order to be a grad transfer with Oklahoma this season. Hurts became the first true freshman quarterback to start at Alabama in over 30 years back in 2016. His overall grade that year ranked 59th among quarterbacks, and he improved that to 24th in 2017. As known, he was then benched for Tua Tagovailoa at halftime of the National Championship that year and subsequently lost his starting job in 2018 and transferred to Oklahoma after spending a year backing up Tagovailoa. Hurts was one of college football’s best quarterbacks in 2019, ranking second to only Joe Burrow in overall grade at 91.6 and got the job done through the air and on the ground. Hurts produced 47 carries of 10-plus yards, which was second to only a triple-option quarterback. The accuracy of Hurts was among the best in the country, as he had an accurate pass rate on throws of 91.6 Hurts held onto the ball longer than any other quarterback and 90.1 performed well under duress, but he won’t get away with that slow time-to-throw and his slow release in the NFL.
blurb2: If there is a path to success for Hurts in the NFL, it's via his combination of legs and protecting the football. His rushing threat can immediately give you an above- average offense if willing to use him creatively, and he's been consistently able to avoid turnovers over the course of his career. The one thing he has not shown that's made offenses like that tick in the league is downfield accuracy. While his legs can bring more defenders up into the box, his arm has not shown he can accurately put balls on receivers down the field to then beat defenses over the top.

name: Jordan Love
blurb1: Tagged as just a three-star quarterback recruit coming out of Bakersfield, California’s Liberty High School, Jordan Love received just five offers, and none of which came from Power 5 programs. The 6-foot-2, 179-pounder ultimately chose Utah State over offers from Eastern Washington, Northern Arizona, Northern Colorado and Sacramento State. As a senior at Liberty, Love completed 50.9% of his passes for 2,148 yards and 24 touchdowns. He also added another 806 rushing yards on 128 carries and eight touchdowns on the ground. Love appeared in 12 games and started six as a redshirt freshman in 2017 and couldn’t get much cooking, posting just a 65.8 passing grade. After lighting up Tennessee Tech, UNLV, New Mexico, etc. in 2018, Love was pegged as a breakout player for 2019 and received first-round hype. Love finished 2019 with a passing grade that ranked 41st among FBS quarterbacks and failed to show up during Utah State’s two games against Power-5 competition. Love’s decision-making was questionable all throughout the year, and he ended up ranking 101st in turnover-worthy play rate. He could hit an open receiver 20-plus yards downfield with ease, and that’s precisely the concerning part of his overall play. Most 75.2 throwing into tight windows, he led the FBS in interceptions. His 82.8 can truly create something out of nothing with his accuracy.
blurb2: It's difficult to blame Love too much for taking a step backward in 2019. He lost his coaching staff and much of his offensive personnel. We've seen time and time again how important situation is for the quarterback position, so expecting him to have better numbers than in 2018 was outrageous. What we can blame him for, though, was how precipitously he fell off. Love very much compounded his bad situation by pressing and trying to do too much within the Utah State offense. While we here at PFF care about on-field performance a ton, the NFL is more lenient, which means Love is still a candidate to go first round.

blurb2: I'm surprised Luton's name hasn't garnered more buzz heading into the draft, given his size and arm talent are both pluses projecting to the NFL. He avoids those mistakes because he's got a bit of Alex Smith in him stylistically. It's rare to see him give any receiver besides Isaiah Hodgins a chance to make a play downfield, and he is very quick to get to his checkdown. Unlike Smith, Luton offers nothing as a runner and was unimpressive when forced outside the pocket. We've seen him improve by leaps and bounds over the years, though, and he put up excellent numbers with very little in the way of NFL talent at Oregon State.

Jefferson also ran track at Destrehan. He was rated as a three-star prospect by 247Sports and Scout. Jefferson come from an athletic family as his two older brothers Jordan and Rickey both started for the LSU football team and Rickey went on to play for the New Orleans Saints. Jefferson’s father, John, played college basketball at Nebraska Western and Northeast Louisiana. Jefferson didn’t have much of an impact in his true freshman season in 2017 – seeing only one target on the season and rushing the ball once for four yards – but his role began to increase as a sophomore in 2018. Jefferson played 697 offensive snaps, primarily out wide, and he served as an effective target in the passing game. He averaged over 16 yards per reception while generating a passer rating when targeted of 121.4 on his 85 targets. Jefferson shifted inside to play 78% of his snaps from the slot TDS receptions (111), receiving yards (1,540) and receiving touchdowns (18). A big part of that was obviously the offensive 85.3 possible, but Jefferson deserves his share of credit as well.
blurb2: One of our biggest motto's at PFF when it comes to draft prospects is that 'we need to see it first'. That basically means we'd like to see a draft prospect do something at a high-level before projecting them to do so in the NFL. Whether that's rush the passer, throw with accuracy, or beat man coverage, we feel more comfortable seeing it. With Jefferson, his massive breakout season was routinely the product of exploiting holes in zone coverage rather than creating space himself. Until we see that, we're just going to be hesitant to covet a prospect too highly.

The 6-foot-2, 183-pound four- star received fielded offers from more than 15 schools, including Georgia, Ole Miss, Michigan, Oklahoma, Auburn and Florida. He originally committed to Georgia but de-committed from the school two weeks before signing day. He then signed with Ole Miss in late January. Jefferson caught over 80 passes with the Rebels before transferring to the University of Florida after the NCAA handed out sanctions to Ole Miss. Jefferson was immediately a starter back at Ole Miss his redshirt freshman season in 2016. That was in a receiving corps that also featured D.K. Metcalf and A.J. Brown, yet it was Jefferson who outproduced both with 49 catches for 543 yards. Fast forward three years later though and Jefferson is still yet to take the next step from a production standpoint even after transferring from Ole Miss to Florida. This past season with the Gators, he only managed 49 catches again for 657 yards with TDS wide receiver friendly, those are rough numbers for career highs.
blurb2: Jefferson will be a difficult evaluation around the NFL for a number of reasons. That's worrisome considering one of his biggest cons is simply play strength which you'd think he'd have an advantage over college corners given his age. On the positive side though, Jefferson has legit speed and consistent hands. He ran away from college corners with ease with free releases. Whether or not he can consistently stack corners from press remains to be seen though.

name: Jerry Jeudy
blurb1: Considered a five-star prospect by Rivals and 247Sports Composite, Jerry Jeudy was one of the most coveted wide receivers in the 2017 recruiting class. He visited the University of Miami (Fla.) and Alabama but ultimately committed to the Crimson Tide in January 2017. Jeudy worked out every other day with fellow Pompano Beach, Florida native and former Alabama star wide receiver Calvin Ridley as a 10th-grader, per John Zenor of AP News. “Great player, works really hard and deserves everything coming his way,” Ridley said in December 2018. “We played high school together and grew up together a little bit. Just seeing him grow and becoming the player he is — that’s the most exciting thing.” Jevon Glenn, Jeudy’s high school football coach at Deerfield, also poured praise onto the young wideout. “He’s got plans, he’s got reservations in his mind to be one of the best when it’s all said and done,” Glenn said. “That explains why he works so hard and why he’s so focused.” Alabama’s wide receiving corps in 2019 was one of the best that college football has ever seen, and Jeudy was the best of that group. He didn’t see a whole lot of opportunity during the 2017 season as a freshman, catching 14 of his 25 targets for 264 yards and two touchdowns. That changed in a big way in 2018 – a season in which Jeudy emerged as on the top wide receivers in the entire country. The 6-foot-1, 192-pound wide receiver racked up over 1,000 yards 86.0 as a sophomore, and then he did the same thing as a junior. One 86.8 in the class is that Jeudy has run the majority of his routes from the slot during his career at Alabama, averaging 3.49 yards per route run
blurb2: There are holes to poke in Jeudy's game for sure, but I'm honestly not sure they really matter. He didn't face press a ton nor did he have a ton of contested targets. You usually feel uneasy when both those things are true about a prospect. That is, unless they were as dominant as Jeudy was in the limited times he saw both. He was too quick for corners at the line of scrimmage and may very well not see much press at the NFL level because of how deadly his speed can be. With how special he is as an athlete, don't expect many corners to be close to him to contest passes in the NFL either.

blurb1: Listed at 6-foot-6, 200 pounds as a four-star recruit coming out California’s Valley Christian High School, Collin Johnson scooped up offers from Texas and Alabama among 10 other Division I programs. He committed to the Longhorns before his junior campaign in April 2014. Johnson suffered a season-ending shoulder injury two games into his senior season in 2015 but still joined Texas as an early enrollee in January 2016. Pre-injury, Johnson caught 49 passes for 921 yards and 11 touchdowns as a junior at Valley Christian, per Texas’ official athletic site. Johnson has recorded 50 or more targets in each of the past four seasons, including his 103-target junior campaign that he turned into 68 receptions for 985 yards, seven touchdowns and an 80.5 PFF receiving grade. He’s dropped just 11 passes across his 306-target career at Texas, and he’s caught north of 60% of his career targets. name: Michael Pittman
blurb1: Michael Pittman Jr. was a standout wide receiver/safety/return specialist at powerhouse Oaks Christian and received national recognition. In 2015, Pittman was named to the Parade All-American first team, Prep Star All-American Dream Team and the Max Preps All-American first team. As a senior, Pittman had 81 receptions for 1,990 yards and 24 touchdowns. On defense he had 31 tackles and an interception, and as a returner he had 477 yards on 17 returns with one touchdown. As a junior, he had 47 receptions for 914 yards and 12 touchdowns, with 43 tackles and three interceptions on defense. Pittman’s father Michael Sr. played in the NFL with the Arizona Cardinals, Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Denver Broncos. Michael’s younger brother Mycah is a freshman wide receiver for the Oregon Ducks. Pittman enjoys riding horses in his spare time. Pittman really didn’t carve out a significant role in USC’s offense until his junior and senior seasons. He totaled just 29 receptions from 44 targets in 2016 and 2017 combined, picking up 486 receiving yards, two touchdowns and just one drop in the process. In 2018, Pittman recorded 100 or more receiving yards in three games (Colorado, Utah, UCLA) and finished the season with 41 receptions from 77 targets for 754 yards and six touchdowns. He also dropped just one pass that season and recorded 236 yards after the catch. 81.2 totaled 101 receptions from 133 targets for 1,269 yards and 11 68.3 also forced a whopping 14 missed tackles after the catch this past season.
blurb2: You'll hear me talk about 'trump cards' throughout the guide. The basic gist of the concept is that a trump card is a skill that a player possesses that is so far and away dominant that you know it will translate to the NFL. For Pittman, that's his ball skills. According to Dawg Nation, he had over 2,000 rushing yards, over 1,500 receiving yards, 50 offensive touchdowns, over 300 tackles and 10 interceptions prior to his senior season. He then proceeded to catch 57 passes – 15 of which were touchdowns – as a senior. That led to Woerner ranking as the 138th overall recruit in the 2016 class and fielding offers from national powers such as Georgia, Alabama, Clemson, Florida, Michigan and Oregon. Woerner committed to Georgia and upheld his commitment despite the firing of Mark Richt. Woerner wasn’t much of a pass catcher over his four-year career at Georgia, ending with just 34 receptions for 376 yards and one touchdown from 2016 to 2019. As a freshman back in that 2016 season, Woerner played 161 offensive snaps, a number that would grow to 294 in 2017, 485 as a junior in 2018 and 662 this past season. The consensus five-star recruit received 33 offers before officially committing to Florida State in April 2015. Per Sanjay Kirpalani of Bleacher Report, Taylor earned a 3.1 GPA at the high school level and recorded a hand-timed 4.28-second 40-yard dash and a 43- inch vertical in the offseason prior to his first year at FSU. Taylor has had an unfortunate last couple of seasons. He broke out in 2017 and was a shutdown outside corner, allowing just 13 of 35 targets to be caught for 162 yards on his 416 coverage snaps with zero touchdowns and four combined interceptions and pass breakups. He battled an injury throughout 2018 and just wasn’t the same player by allowing over a yard per coverage snap and four total touchdowns. Taylor was then moved to safety in 2019 and struggled in that role by posting a 63.3 coverage grade, which was far lower than his previous two seasons. TKLS
blurb2: I get why a 5-foot-10, 190-pounder like Taylor would want to move to safety/slot in an effort to increase his draft stock, but I truly believed that he could be one of the few to overcome those size deficiencies on the outside, and he'd pretty much already done that performance-wise. Now, he wouldn't be a fit in every scheme, but he has easy speed, movement skills and leaping ability to make up for his stature. Switching to safety and then the slot this year, Taylor looked like someone who really hadn't played either. name: Safety
blurb1: K’Von Wallace, a three-star safety recruit coming out of Virginia’s Highland Springs High School in 2016, held official visits with Clemson and Ohio State before committing to the Tigers in February 2016, per 247Sports. He was both a track star and football standout at Highland Springs. As a senior, he received first-team all-state honors at wide receiver and defensive back. Wallace has been used all over the field in his time at Clemson and been consistent over the last three years, posting overall grades in the low 80s in each season. In 2019 specifically, Wallace took his game to another level by recording a career-high 89.7 coverage grade. He wasn’t much of a ballhawk in coverage prior to this year as he recorded just nine combined pass breakups and interceptions from 2016-18 but improved in that area by producing 10 in 2019. Wallace fits the prototypical dimeback player at the NFL level. TKLS
blurb2: If you were to build an ideal slot corner, it would look a lot like Wallace. You want someone with enough size to blow up receiver screens. Wallace checks in at 5-11, 205 pounds. You want someone who can react quickly and break up passes underneath. Wallace had eight pass breakups last year. And finally, you want someone who has some savvy in reading routes. Wallace has been manning the slot at Clemson for three straight seasons and earned exceptional coverage grades in each. At that point, we're going to be fans of Wallace's game.

name: Antoine Winfield
blurb1: The son of former NFL standout Antoine Winfield, Winfield Jr. began his high-school career at Eden Prairie before transferring to The Woodlands. In his senior season there, he recorded 87 tackles, five forced fumbles and two interceptions per the Minnesota official athletics’ website. He was named Montgomery County Player of the Year during that senior season. As a three- star recruit, Winfield had offers to eight schools – Minnesota, Eastern Michigan, Houston, Lamar, Missouri, Northwestern, Purdue and SMU – and he committed to Minnesota after visiting in December. Winfield’s football career was starting to go south after he had to seek medical redshirts in both 2017 and 2018. However, he defied the odds and came back as one of college football’s best safeties in 2019. Winfield produced the seventh-best coverage grade among draft-eligible safeties at 89.2, and he generated nine combined forced incompletions and interceptions, the same number of first downs that he allowed on throws into his primary coverage.. blurb2: While Winfield's seven picks this past season are a bit inflated by some lucky bounces, they are indicative of the playmaking ability he brings to the safety position. He can go from single-high to split-field to the slot and make plays on the football no matter the role. Unlike a lot of playmakers though, Winfield's picks don't come from guessing or jumping routes willy-nilly. No, Winfield is just darn good at splitting routes and being precisely where he needs to be on the back end. From that perspective, don't expect too steep of a learning curve for Winfield once he gets to the league.
